title: Chest flutters in a 69-year-old teacher
desc: This station is a focused palpitations history and cardiovascular examination of Philip Miller, a 69-year-old history teacher. He presents to a rural emergency department with 40 minutes of sudden, racing ‘chest flutters’, light-headedness and central chest tightness. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, 12-lead ECG and blood results. They should diagnose new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response that started less than 48 hours ago in a haemodynamically stable patient, then outline rate control, stroke risk and anticoagulation, the place of cardioversion and the disposition. Finally they answer his fear of a heart attack, including the complications of AF and safety netting.
focus: Palpitations: a structured history with cluster questions, then recognising and managing new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (new onset, under 48 hours)
stem: You are a third-year medical student on your emergency medicine rotation at a busy rural hospital. Philip Miller, a 69-year-old man, has come in with 40 minutes of ongoing ‘chest flutters’. The triage nurse has put him on a bed in the acute area and is available to help you. The triage nurse has inserted a cannula and sent bloods. A 12-lead ECG has not yet been recorded and he is not yet on a cardiac monitor. The ED registrar has asked you to see him first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Miller and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, his 12-lead ECG and his blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Philip Miller, a 69-year-old high school history teacher. You are sitting up on the ED bed. You are uncomfortable and a bit anxious, and every so often you put a hand on your chest. You talk in full sentences. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: “Hi, thanks for seeing me. I came into the hospital today because I can feel ‘flutters’ inside my chest.”

The palpitations (give only when asked):

  • What it feels like: “chest flutters”. You can feel your heart beating inside your chest, and it is racing. It is an uncomfortable feeling.
  • Tapping it out: if the candidate asks you to tap out the rhythm, tap fast and unevenly and say, “It's hard to tap, it's all over the place.”
  • Onset: it came on quite suddenly while you were sitting marking your students' essays at the kitchen table. You weren't doing anything strenuous.
  • Duration: it started about 40 minutes ago and has not stopped. Your wife drove you in.
  • First episode: you have never had anything like this before.
  • Better or worse: nothing makes it better or worse.
  • Radiation: it doesn't go anywhere.
  • Impact: it was so uncomfortable that you had to stop marking.

Associated symptoms (only if asked):

  • Light-headedness: “In the ED waiting room I started feeling a bit light-headed.” You have not fainted or nearly fainted.
  • Chest: “a bit of tightness in the centre of my chest”. It is not pain, just discomfort. It does not spread to your arm, jaw or back, and it is not crushing. No sweating, nausea or vomiting.
  • Breathing: not short of breath. You can lie flat and you have no ankle swelling.
  • Possible triggers: two cups of coffee a day, no more than usual today. No alcohol today and no recent heavy drinking. No recent illness. You have been eating and drinking normally. No energy drinks, cold and flu tablets or recreational drugs.
  • Infection: no cough, phlegm, cold symptoms, fever, sweats or shivers. No sharp pain on breathing in. No sick contacts.
  • Thyroid: no neck swelling, no weight loss, no trouble with the heat, no change in appetite, no diarrhoea, no shakiness or nervousness.
  • Mood: no anxiety, panic attacks or recent stress beyond the usual end-of-term marking.
  • Stroke or bleeding (only if asked): no weakness, numbness, speech or vision problems, ever. No bleeding problems, stomach ulcers or black stools.

Past medical history:

  • High blood pressure. You are not sure whether it is well controlled because you don't check it regularly.
  • High cholesterol.
  • Appendix removed at 21.
  • No heart attack, heart failure, valve problems, stroke, mini-stroke, diabetes or kidney problems.
  • No angina, and you have never had chest pain or tightness on exertion before today.
  • No circulation problems or cramping pain in your legs when walking, and no aortic problems.

Medications: perindopril arginine 10 mg and rosuvastatin 40 mg, both once a day by mouth. No blood thinners, over-the-counter medicines or supplements. No recreational drugs.

Allergies: penicillin. “I break out in hives when I have penicillin.”

Family history:

  • Your mother is 93 and lives in high-level care with Alzheimer's dementia.
  • Your father died at 70 of a stroke caused by a clot.
  • Your brother Fred is 63 and well.
  • Your two sons, John and Timothy, are both well.
  • No one in the family died suddenly or young, and no one has a known heart rhythm problem.

Social history:

  • Smoking: never.
  • Alcohol: socially, 1 to 2 glasses of red wine on weekends.
  • Work: high school history teacher.
  • Exercise: you walk for 30 to 40 minutes 3 days a week.
  • Diet: takeaway most nights.
  • Home: you live with your wife. Your sons have moved out but live within a 30-minute drive. You have a strong support network.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • You think this might be the early sign of a heart attack: “I'm worried that this could be an early sign of a heart attack.”
  • You are worried it could stop you teaching your classes.
  • You want to know what is going on and whether it is your heart.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1, if not already covered: “Is this a heart attack?”

How Philip changes:

  • If the candidate asks whether an ECG has been done, the nurse says, “Not yet.”
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, the nurse says, “I'll do it now”, and the examiner hands it over in Part 2.
  • If the candidate asks for cardiac monitoring, the nurse attaches it and says the monitor shows a fast, irregular rhythm at about 130.
  • If he is asked to stand, he feels more light-headed. Otherwise he stays the same throughout Part 1.
  • If the candidate is calm and explains what they are doing, he settles a little.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: alert, mildly anxious man sitting up and talking in full sentences. Not pale, sweaty or cyanosed. Weight 88 kg.
  • Vital signs (13:50): HR 132 beats/min, irregular (apical count by the triage nurse; the pulse oximeter is reading a fluctuating 110 to 125; not yet on a cardiac monitor). BP 128/80 mmHg. RR 18/min. SpO2 97% on room air. Temperature 36.8 °C. Bedside glucose 6.0 mmol/L.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds. No tremor. Not hot or sweaty. No clubbing or peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.
  • Radial pulse: about 118/min, irregularly irregular, with beat-to-beat variation in volume. If the candidate counts the apex rate at the same time, it is 132/min (a pulse deficit of about 14). No radio-radial delay.
  • Face, eyes and neck: no pallor. No lid lag, lid retraction or exophthalmos. No goitre or thyroid nodules. Carotid pulses normal in character, no bruits. JVP 2 cm above the sternal angle.
  • Praecordium: no scars. Apex beat in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line, not displaced. No heaves or thrills. S1 varies in intensity, S2 is normal. No murmurs, added sounds or rub, including in the left lateral position.
  • Chest: resonant, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles, wheeze or bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Healed right iliac fossa appendicectomy scar.
  • Legs: no pitting oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.
  • Neurological screen (if asked): no facial droop, no limb weakness, speech normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self (name and role as a medical student), confirms Philip's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Acknowledges his discomfort and his fear of a heart attack, uses plain language, keeps the history focused because he is symptomatic, and summarises back to him.
History
Characterises the palpitations:

kids.x: What it feels like: a racing heart he can feel inside his chest; asks him to tap out the rhythm (fast and irregular, hard to tap).
Onset and duration: sudden onset at rest while marking essays, about 40 minutes ago, continuous since.
kids.d: The time of onset is critical: it sets the 48-hour window for cardioversion.

kids.x: First ever episode; nothing makes it better or worse; no radiation.
Impact: had to stop marking because of the discomfort.

check.x: Asks about symptoms of haemodynamic compromise:

kids.x: Light-headedness, presyncope or syncope (light-headed in the waiting room, no faint).
Chest pain: characterises the central tightness as discomfort, not crushing, not radiating, with no sweating or nausea.

check.x: Asks about precipitants: caffeine, alcohol (including binges), stimulants or recreational drugs, recent infection and dehydration (none beyond his usual two coffees).
Uses cluster questions to screen the differentials beyond a tachyarrhythmia:
check.d: Source marking: full credit for tachyarrhythmia questions plus clusters for 3 other differentials; part credit for 1 or 2. Item 6 counts as the tachyarrhythmia cluster.

kids.x: Myocardial infarction: character and radiation of the chest discomfort, sweating, nausea, exertional pattern, and previous angina or MI.
Pneumonia: cough, coryza, sputum, pleuritic pain, fever or rigors, sick contacts (none).
Hyperthyroidism: neck swelling, weight loss, heat intolerance, increased appetite, diarrhoea, nervousness (none).
Anxiety disorder: agitation, social stressors, panic attacks (none).

check.x: Past medical history: hypertension (not monitored, control unknown), hypercholesterolaemia and appendicectomy at 21.
Asks specifically about stroke and bleeding risk factors: previous stroke or TIA, heart failure, diabetes, vascular disease, valve disease and any history of bleeding (all absent).
check.d: Needed to calculate CHA2DS2-VA and plan anticoagulation. Credit if the candidate asks about previous stroke or TIA and any bleeding history, plus at least two of heart failure, diabetes, vascular disease or valve disease.

check.x: Medications: perindopril arginine 10 mg and rosuvastatin 40 mg daily; no anticoagulants, over-the-counter medicines, supplements or recreational drugs.
Allergies: penicillin, with the reaction (hives).
Family history: father died at 70 of an ischaemic stroke, mother 93 with Alzheimer's dementia, brother and sons well; no sudden or premature cardiac deaths.
Takes a social history:
check.d: Source marking: 2 marks for social history.

kids.x: Never smoked; alcohol quantified (1 to 2 glasses of red wine on weekends).
Occupation (history teacher), exercise (walks 3 days a week), diet (takeaway most nights), lives with his wife, strong support.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it may be an early heart attack, worries about teaching, wants to know what is going on.
Examination
Asks the nurse early for a 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring (before finishing the examination).
check.d: Credit if the candidate either asks for an ECG or asks whether one has been done and requests it.

check.x: Asks for vital signs and states he is tachycardic but not hypotensive, hypoxic or febrile (haemodynamically stable at present); bedside glucose is a bonus.
Examines the pulse:

kids.x: Radial rate and rhythm: identifies a fast, irregularly irregular pulse (variable volume is a bonus).
Compares the apex rate with the radial rate and identifies a pulse deficit (132 against about 118).

check.x: General inspection and perfusion: conscious state, pallor, sweating, warm peripheries and capillary refill.
Examines the praecordium for valve disease and structural heart disease: apex beat, heaves, heart sounds and murmurs (none; variable S1).
Looks for heart failure and infection: JVP, lung bases for crackles, breath sounds and peripheral oedema (all normal).
Looks for thyrotoxicosis: tremor, warm sweaty hands, lid lag or exophthalmos, and goitre (none).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: HR 128 to 134 irregular in the yellow (clinical review) zone at every set, with BP, RR, SpO2, temperature and conscious state normal; still haemodynamically stable, but the rate is not settling on its own.
Reads the ECG systematically (patient details, rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, ST segments):
check.d: Source marking: patient details, absent P waves, irregularly irregular rhythm, rapid ventricular rate about 132.

kids.x: Absent P waves with fibrillatory waves (naming the lead is not required).
Rapid ventricular rate of about 132 with narrow QRS complexes, normal axis and no acute ischaemic ST change.

check.x: Concludes new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, onset clearly under 48 hours, haemodynamically stable.

Interprets the bloods: normal TSH and free T4 (not thyrotoxic), normal K and Mg, normal Hb, normal WCC and CRP (no infection), hs-troponin normal at 0 hours but needs a repeat, and creatinine, eGFR and coagulation as a baseline for anticoagulation.
Calculates his stroke risk: CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 (age 65 to 74, hypertension), so oral anticoagulation is recommended.
check.d: Accept CHA2DS2-VASc of 2 (same for a man).

check.x: Gives at least two differentials, each with a feature for or against (ACS, atrial flutter, thyrotoxicosis, infection, anxiety).
Management

States he is stable (no hypotension, shock, heart failure, ischaemia or syncope), so emergency electrical cardioversion is not needed, and that synchronised DC cardioversion would be used if he became unstable.
Immediate care: continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access, repeat observations, and escalation to the ED senior or medical registrar.

Rate control: a beta-blocker (for example metoprolol IV or oral) or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil IV, or oral diltiazem or verapamil), aiming for a resting HR below 110; digoxin is reserved mainly for heart failure.
Rhythm control: because onset is clearly under 48 hours, discusses pharmacological or electrical cardioversion with the senior or cardiology team, with anticoagulation started first.
Anticoagulation: starts a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban or dabigatran) in preference to warfarin because the AF is non-valvular, not aspirin; checks renal function and bleeding risk first.
Repeat troponin at 15:45 and arrange an echocardiogram.
Disposition: ED short stay with cardiology input; discharge if reverted or rate-controlled with a negative repeat troponin, otherwise admit; GP follow-up for BP, alcohol, weight and sleep apnoea.
Answers Philip in plain words: the top chambers of the heart are beating chaotically and fast; the ECG and first blood test do not show a heart attack, but the test is being repeated.
Names at least two complications of AF, including thromboembolism and stroke; others are haemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest and, in the long term, heart failure.
Safety netting
Gives the red flags in plain words: chest pain that is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes, fainting, severe breathlessness, or signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, trouble speaking).

Says what to do and where: while in hospital, press the call bell or tell the nurse straight away if any of these happen; after discharge, call 000. Bonus: bleeding or a head injury on the blood thinner, go to ED.

part2.lead: It is now 14:55. Here are Philip's observations since he arrived, the 12-lead ECG the nurse recorded at 13:52, and his blood results.
part2.patient:
Philip is still on the bed with palpitations. When the candidate reaches the fourth question, Philip asks it himself: “Is this a heart attack, and could it be dangerous?”

He is reassured by a clear, honest explanation. If the candidate uses jargon such as “rapid ventricular response” or “anticoagulation” without explaining it, he asks what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: ED observations, on room air throughout. Cardiac monitoring in place since 13:55.
handover.model:
Read: HR 132, 128 and 134, irregular, at the three sets. BP 128/80, 126/78 and 124/76 mmHg. RR 18 to 20. SpO2 96 to 97% on room air. Temperature 36.8 to 36.9 °C. Alert, with chest discomfort of 1 to 2 out of 10.

Chart zones: on the NSW adult chart, HR of 128 to 134 sits in the yellow zone (clinical review) at every set. BP, RR, SpO2, temperature and conscious state are all in the white zone, and nothing reaches the red (rapid response) zone.

For Philip: a persisting irregular tachycardia, now about 1 hour 45 minutes after onset, with no hypotension, hypoxaemia, fever or altered conscious state. He is haemodynamically stable, but he is not reverting or slowing on his own.

What it changes: the yellow-zone heart rate needs medical review now. He does not need emergency DC cardioversion. He needs rate control and continued monitoring, with escalation if his BP falls, he faints, or the chest pain or breathlessness worsens.

rows.note: On arrival in acute bed; palpitations and chest tightness
Repeat set: still palpitations, light-headed on sitting up

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (13:52)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, recorded at 13:52 by the ED nurse during palpitations. Philip Miller, 69, male. Standard calibration (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: ventricular rate about 132 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: irregularly irregular. RR intervals vary throughout, with no repeating pattern.
  • P waves: absent. Irregular fibrillatory waves on the baseline, best seen in V1 and the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). No sawtooth flutter waves.
  • Axis: normal (+30°).
  • PR interval: not measurable.
  • QRS: 88 ms, narrow. No bundle branch block. No left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage.
  • QT: QTc about 430 ms (averaged over several beats).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. No T wave inversion. No pathological Q waves.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.

Conclusion: irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 132 beats/min with absent P waves and fibrillatory waves. No acute ischaemic changes.
handover.model:
Read: confirms the patient details. Rate about 132. Irregularly irregular rhythm. Absent P waves with fibrillatory waves, best seen in V1 and the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Normal axis, narrow QRS, QTc normal. No ST or T change.

For Philip: this is atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. There are no regular flutter waves (against atrial flutter) and no distinct P waves of several shapes (against multifocal atrial tachycardia). There is no ischaemic change, and the chest tightness fits a rate-related symptom, but one ECG does not exclude ACS. A clear onset 40 minutes before arrival puts him well within 48 hours.

What it changes: start rate control and calculate his stroke risk for anticoagulation. Because onset is under 48 hours, cardioversion is an option, to discuss with a senior. Repeat the ECG if the chest pain changes and when the rhythm or rate changes.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 13:45 on arrival in ED. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: FBC normal (Hb 146). Na, K 4.2 and Mg 0.86 are normal. Creatinine 92 with eGFR 74. TSH 1.8 and free T4 14, both normal. CRP 2 and WCC 7.4. Glucose 6.0. INR 1.0 and APTT 31. ALT normal. hs-troponin T 11 ng/L, below the 99th centile.

For Philip: there is no thyrotoxicosis, electrolyte disturbance, anaemia or infection driving the AF. The troponin was taken only about 35 minutes after symptom onset, so a single normal value does not exclude myocardial injury and it must be repeated. Normal renal function (estimated creatinine clearance about 80 mL/min), a normal INR and a normal Hb mean a DOAC can be started at full dose.

What it changes: work-up continues with a repeat troponin and an echocardiogram. With a CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 (age 65 to 74 and hypertension), oral anticoagulation is recommended, and nothing in these results prevents it.

rows.n: Collected about 35 minutes after symptom onset; repeat sample due 15:45

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Philip, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Philip now, here in the emergency department.

Philip asks you: “Is this a heart attack, and could it be dangerous?” Please answer him, including the complications of this condition, the warning signs he should watch for and what he should do if they happen.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student in ED. Philip Miller, 69.
  • Situation: new-onset AF with a rapid ventricular response, onset at about 13:10 (under 2 hours ago), haemodynamically stable.
  • Background: first episode. Light-headed, central chest tightness. Hypertension (control unknown), hypercholesterolaemia. Takes perindopril and rosuvastatin. Penicillin allergy (hives). No anticoagulant.
  • Assessment: HR 128 to 134 irregular (yellow zone), BP 124 to 128 systolic, SpO2 96 to 97% RA, afebrile, alert. No heart failure signs or murmur. ECG: AF about 132, narrow QRS, no ischaemic change. Bloods: TSH and fT4, K, Mg, Hb and CRP normal; 0-hour hs-troponin 11, repeat due; eGFR 74. CHA2DS2-VA 2.
  • Recommendation: please review. Rate control, start a DOAC, consider cardioversion (under 48 hours), repeat troponin, echo, decide on disposition.

Most likely: new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, under 48 hours, haemodynamically stable. For it: sudden irregular racing palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse with a deficit, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves and irregular RR at about 132.

  • ACS (must exclude): chest tightness, age and risk factors. Against: not crushing or radiating, no ST change, normal 0-hour troponin; repeat needed.
  • Atrial flutter with variable block: against: no sawtooth waves, totally irregular rhythm.
  • Thyrotoxicosis as a trigger: against: no symptoms or signs, normal TSH and fT4.
  • Infection as a trigger: against: afebrile, clear chest, normal WCC and CRP.
  • Anxiety: against: objective arrhythmia on ECG.

1. Stable (no hypotension, shock, heart failure, ischaemia or syncope), so no emergency DC cardioversion. If he becomes unstable, synchronised DC cardioversion.
  2. Monitor: cardiac monitoring, IV access, repeat observations; escalate to the ED senior or medical registrar.
  3. Rate control: a beta-blocker (for example metoprolol IV or oral) or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil IV, or oral diltiazem or verapamil); target resting HR below 110.
  4. Rhythm control: onset under 48 hours, so pharmacological or electrical cardioversion is an option, discussed with a senior or cardiology, with anticoagulation first.
  5. Anticoagulation: CHA2DS2-VA 2, so start a DOAC (for example apixaban), not aspirin, after checking renal function and bleeding risk.
  6. Work-up: repeat troponin at 15:45 and arrange an echocardiogram.
  7. Disposition: ED short stay with cardiology input; discharge if reverted or rate-controlled with a negative repeat troponin, otherwise admit; GP follow-up for BP, alcohol, weight and sleep apnoea.

• Plain words: the top chambers of his heart are beating chaotically, making the heart race and beat irregularly. The ECG and first blood test do not show a heart attack, but the test is being repeated.
  • Complications (at least two): clots forming in the heart that can cause a stroke (his father's illness); low blood pressure or fainting; rarely, cardiac arrest; heart failure in the long term if the rate is not controlled.
  • Warning signs: chest pain that is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes, fainting, severe breathlessness, face drooping, arm weakness or trouble speaking.
  • What to do: while in hospital, press the call bell or tell the nurse straight away if any of these happen; after discharge, call 000.
  • Bonus, on a blood thinner: bleeding or a head injury, go to ED.

ddx.dx: New-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (onset under 48 hours, haemodynamically stable)
ddx.for: Sudden racing palpitations at rest for 40 minutes that he cannot tap out, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, and an ECG with absent P waves, fibrillatory waves and irregular RR intervals at about 132.
Central chest tightness with light-headedness in a 69-year-old with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and a takeaway diet.
ddx.against: Discomfort that is not crushing or radiating, no sweating or nausea, no ischaemic ST change and a normal 0-hour hs-troponin, which still needs repeating.

ddx.for: A rapid narrow-complex tachycardia with an irregular pulse.
ddx.against: No sawtooth flutter waves, and the RR intervals are irregular with no repeating pattern.

ddx.for: New AF in an older adult.
ddx.against: No weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, goitre or eye signs, with a normal TSH and free T4.

ddx.dx: Infection (such as pneumonia) precipitating atrial fibrillation
ddx.for: Infection is a common trigger of new AF.
ddx.against: No cough, sputum, fever or sick contacts, a clear chest, temperature 36.8 °C and normal WCC and CRP.

ddx.for: He is worried and this is his first episode.
ddx.against: No stressors, panic attacks or nervousness, and the ECG shows an objective arrhythmia.

guide:
Part 1: allow about 6 minutes for the history and 4 for the examination. Prompt “please move on to your examination” at about 6 minutes if needed. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Give the apex rate (and so the pulse deficit) only if the candidate counts the apex. Item 8 follows the source marking: full credit for the tachyarrhythmia cluster (item 6) plus cluster questions for 3 other differentials, and part credit for 1 or 2. Credit item 10 if the candidate asks about previous stroke or TIA and any bleeding history, plus at least two of heart failure, diabetes, vascular disease or valve disease. Credit item 17 if, before the examination is finished, the candidate either asks for an ECG or asks whether one has been done and requests it.

Part 2: hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Philip asks the fourth question himself. Credit the ECG read (items 26 and 27) in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer, and credit the CHA2DS2-VA score wherever it is given. The source case asked only for two complications of AF (item 40). The full rate and rhythm control drug choices are teaching and are not all expected; credit item 34 for one correct rate-control class with the HR target.

A high-performing candidate pins down the exact time of onset, asks about light-headedness and chest pain, screens the differentials in clusters, and asks about stroke and bleeding risk. They ask for an ECG early and find the irregularly irregular pulse with a deficit. In Part 2 they read the ECG systematically and name stable AF under 48 hours. They calculate CHA2DS2-VA as 2, give rate control with a target, start a DOAC, explain the 48-hour rule for cardioversion and repeat the troponin. They reassure Philip honestly and name stroke as the key complication.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history without the time of onset, misses the pulse deficit, calls the ECG “sinus tachycardia” or “SVT”, or plans immediate electrical cardioversion in a stable patient without considering anticoagulation. They may prescribe aspirin for stroke prevention or tell him it is definitely not his heart.
explain:
The diagnosis: new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia. The atria are activated rapidly and chaotically, so atrial contraction is uncoordinated, and the AV node conducts irregularly to the ventricles. Philip has a sudden onset of racing palpitations at rest, 40 minutes before he was seen. He cannot tap out the rhythm, he is light-headed and his chest feels tight. His pulse is irregularly irregular with a pulse deficit, and the ECG shows absent P waves, fibrillatory waves and irregular RR intervals at about 132 beats/min. He is haemodynamically stable: alert, BP 124 to 128 systolic, no heart failure and no ischaemic ECG change. The documented onset is well under 48 hours.

Taking the history

  • Characterise the palpitations: onset (sudden or gradual), duration, first or recurrent, and the rhythm (ask the patient to tap it out). The exact time of onset matters because it decides whether early cardioversion is safe.
  • Ask about haemodynamic compromise: light-headedness, syncope, chest pain and breathlessness.
  • Ask about triggers: alcohol, caffeine, stimulants, infection, dehydration and thyroid disease.
  • Screen the differentials in clusters:
    • myocardial infarction: character and radiation of the chest discomfort, sweating, nausea, exertional pattern, and previous angina or MI;
    • pneumonia: cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, fever;
    • hyperthyroidism: weight loss, heat intolerance, diarrhoea, goitre;
    • anxiety: stressors and panic attacks.
  • Look for stroke and bleeding risk in the background: hypertension, age, previous stroke or TIA, heart failure, diabetes, vascular disease and any bleeding history.

Reading the ECG

The three features of AF are absent P waves (often with a fine or coarse fibrillatory baseline), an irregularly irregular rhythm, and, when untreated, a rapid ventricular rate. Two conditions can look similar:

  • Atrial flutter with variable block: sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, with RR intervals that are multiples of the flutter cycle.
  • Multifocal atrial tachycardia: distinct P waves of at least three shapes, usually in severe lung disease.

Always look for ischaemic changes, pre-excitation and QT prolongation, which change the choice of drug.

Results

A normal TSH and free T4, potassium, magnesium, Hb, WCC and CRP make thyrotoxicosis, an electrolyte disturbance, anaemia and infection unlikely triggers. A single normal hs-troponin taken 35 minutes after onset does not exclude myocardial injury, so it is repeated. Renal function, a normal INR and Hb are the baseline for anticoagulation. A transthoracic echocardiogram assesses LV function, valve disease and atrial size.

Acute management (eTG Cardiovascular; NHFA/CSANZ AF guideline 2018)

  • Haemodynamically unstable (hypotension, shock, syncope, acute heart failure, ongoing ischaemia): urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion.
  • Stable: cardiac monitoring, IV access and treatment of any trigger, then rate or rhythm control.
    • Rate control: a beta-blocker (for example metoprolol IV or oral) or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil IV, or oral diltiazem or verapamil). Digoxin is used mainly in heart failure; calcium channel blockers should be avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Aim initially for a resting HR below 110 (lenient rate control).
    • Rhythm control: pharmacological cardioversion with flecainide (only without structural or ischaemic heart disease, and given with a beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) or amiodarone, or synchronised electrical cardioversion under sedation. Sotalol is used to maintain sinus rhythm, not to cardiovert. Contraindications mean not every drug suits every patient. Many first episodes revert on their own within 24 to 48 hours.
  • Cardioversion and the 48-hour rule: if AF has lasted under 48 hours, cardioversion can be done once anticoagulation has started. If it has lasted 48 hours or more, or the duration is unknown, either exclude left atrial thrombus with a transoesophageal echocardiogram first, or give 3 to 4 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation before cardioversion, then continue it for at least 4 weeks afterwards. Newer international guidance (ESC 2024) uses a 24-hour threshold, and the shorter the duration the lower the risk; Philip, at under 2 hours, is within both.

Stroke prevention

The source uses CHA2DS2-VASc. The Australian 2018 guideline uses CHA2DS2-VA, which leaves out female sex. The points are:

  • congestive heart failure 1;
  • hypertension 1;
  • age 75 or over 2;
  • diabetes 1;
  • previous stroke, TIA or thromboembolism 2;
  • vascular disease 1;
  • age 65 to 74 1.

Philip scores 2 (age 65 to 74 and hypertension). Oral anticoagulation is recommended for a score of 2 or more and should be considered for a score of 1. In non-valvular AF, a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban or dabigatran) is preferred to warfarin. Apixaban is 5 mg twice daily unless the patient meets two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 µmol/L or more. Warfarin is needed for moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. Assess bleeding risk to correct modifiable factors (uncontrolled blood pressure, alcohol excess, interacting drugs), not as a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

Complications of AF

  • Thromboembolism, especially stroke, from clot forming in the stagnant left atrial appendage.
  • Haemodynamic instability.
  • Cardiac arrest.
  • In the long term, heart failure, including tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.

Answering Philip's questions

  • Is this a heart attack: it is an irregular, fast rhythm from the top chambers of the heart. The heart tracing and first blood test do not show a heart attack, but we repeat the blood test to be sure, so I cannot say it is definitely not your heart yet.
  • Why a blood thinner: his age and blood pressure put his stroke risk at a level where a blood thinner clearly lowers it. The stroke it prevents is the same kind of clot-related stroke his father had, and aspirin does not protect against it.
  • Teaching: when he can go back to work is decided at review, once the heart rate or rhythm is controlled and the tests are complete.

Disposition, risk factors and safety netting

A stable patient can be observed in ED or short stay. Discharge is reasonable once the rhythm has reverted or the rate is controlled and myocardial injury is excluded; otherwise he is admitted. Senior and cardiology input is needed, by telehealth at a rural site if necessary. The Australian guideline stresses integrated care: control of blood pressure, weight, alcohol and sleep apnoea, and physical activity reduce the AF burden.

Safety netting:

  • While in hospital, press the call bell or tell the nurse straight away for chest pain, fainting, breathlessness or signs of stroke.
  • After discharge, call 000 for severe, worsening or 10-minute chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness or signs of stroke.
  • Go to ED for bleeding or a head injury on the anticoagulant.
  • See the GP within a week with the discharge letter, and have cardiology review with an echocardiogram.
points: Pin down the exact time of onset of palpitations: under 48 hours allows early cardioversion once anticoagulation has started, while 48 hours or more (or unknown) needs a TOE or 3 to 4 weeks of anticoagulation first. Newer guidance (ESC 2024) uses 24 hours; Philip, at under 2 hours, is within both.

AF on ECG has absent P waves (fibrillatory waves), an irregularly irregular rhythm and, when untreated, a rapid ventricular rate. An irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit is the bedside clue.

Unstable AF (hypotension, shock, syncope, heart failure, ischaemia) needs synchronised DC cardioversion. Stable AF needs monitoring, treatment of triggers and rate control with a beta-blocker or diltiazem or verapamil, aiming for a resting HR below 110.
Use CHA2DS2-VA to decide on anticoagulation: a score of 2 or more means anticoagulate, preferably with a DOAC in non-valvular AF. Aspirin is not for stroke prevention in AF.
Look for triggers and mimics: ACS (repeat the troponin), thyrotoxicosis, infection, electrolytes and alcohol.
Complications of AF are stroke and other thromboembolism, haemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest and, in the long term, heart failure.
